column1: # THE SAILS. One row per sail a captain can buy.
# Edit here, then: npm run import && npm run catalogue
# A sail belongs to ONE category and fits a berth of that category. That is the whole fitting rule.
# Area is not the category: a lateen can rival a course and a staysail is a scrap, and both are TRI.
#   LSQ  Large square    courses, lower topsails            driving power, low on the mast
#   SSQ  Small square    topgallants, royals, skysails,     light-air lift, high up
#                        spritsails, sprit-topsails
#   TRI  Headsail        jibs, flying jibs, staysails       set on a stay forward: balance, pointing
#   LAT  Lateen          lateen yards, Bermuda mainsails    triangular canvas driving from a mast
#   GAF  Gaff            gaff mainsails, spankers,          fore-and-aft drive aft, manoeuvre
#                        drivers, trysails, gaff topsails
#   LUG  Lugsail         dipping and standing lug,          the main drive of a lugger
#                        lug topsail
#   STU  Studdingsail    boomed-out extensions             ADDITIVE. Not a berth: see below.
# STU does not go in a berth. A studdingsail booms out beyond a square sail that is already set and
# its area comes off that sail, so it is an attachment rather than a place in the rig. Nothing models
# that yet and `npm run catalogue` refuses a berth that asks for one, deliberately, so that a mast
# cannot pretend to carry studdingsails in a slot.
# id      short camelCase name, unique.
# name    what a captain reads.
# kind    one of the six labels above.
# price   coins.
# drive   what she pulls, as a share of a course's. Physical area is where this number starts, and
#         the proportions to use are: course 1.00, lower topsail 0.70, topgallant 0.40, royal 0.22,
#         skysail 0.12, studdingsail 0.50 to 0.80 of the square sail it booms out from. Better cloth
#         holds its shape and adds to it, which is why two sails of one area can differ here.
# hand    what it does to her helm. Square canvas stiffens her, so it is negative; fore-and-aft
#         canvas helps her round, so it is positive.
# blurb   one line a captain reads.
# These eight are placeholders standing in until the real sail list arrives. Their categories are
# right; their prices and figures are only placed relative to each other.
id
course
column7: The big lower sail. Plain flax, and it pulls.

column1: courseFine
column7: The same sail in heavier cloth. Holds its shape when the plain one is bellying out of it.

column1: topsail
column7: Half the cloth of a course, and it sits where the wind is cleaner.

column1: topsailFine
column7: A topsail worth setting in weather that would split the plain one.

column1: staysail
column7: A small triangle set on a stay. Not much pull, and she feels it in the rudder.

column1: staysailFine
column7: The staysail a captain keeps when she changes ships.

column1: lateen
column7: A long triangle on a raking yard. Less pull than a course, and she comes round on it.

column1: lateenFine
column7: Cut flat rather than full, so it holds an edge to the wind the plain one spills.
